newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Peronists change tune on Congress' jobless debate.
newsitem.headline: Peronists change tune on Congress' jobless debate.

text.p: Argentina's ruling Peronist Party agreed on Tuesday to join an opposition-sponsored debate on unemployment in the lower house of Congress scheduled for 1430 local time (1730 GMT) Wednesday.

Jorge Matzkin, Peronist whip in the Chamber of Deputies, had ruled out granting a quorum to the debate proposed by the Frepaso and Radical opposition, saying his party "is not going to dance to the Frepaso's tune like the Radicals do."
But Matzkin changed his tune on Tuesday, telling reporters: "We will go to the house tomorrow to join the debate on unemployment."

The opposition had accused Peronists of trying to avoid debate on Argentina's hottest social issue -- unemployment of 17.1 percent. Frepaso leader Carlos "Chacho" Alvarez wants the debate to result in a "plebiscite...so that everyone can have a strong involvement in the debate on unemployment."
"I want the country to debate in three or four months' time economic and social policy to improve the job situation," Alvarez told a meeting of opposition groups.
The Radical whip in the lower house Federico Storani told the meeting he wanted "the debate to result in a commitment to discuss a law on employment in no more than two weeks."

The Radical acknowledged this clashed head-on with the Peronist government's plans to make labor legislation more flexible by scrapping collective pay deals, making part of wages dependent on economic health and swapping redundancy payouts for unemployment insurance schemes.

Radicals and the Frepaso both backed last week's 36-hour general strike by unions protesting labor and fiscal austerity measures and demanding a response to the job crisis. They both staged a nationwide "blackout" protest last month.
Frepaso leader Alvarez read out a letter inviting Peronist President Carlos Menem to the unemployment debate in Congress.

But Menem declined the offer, telling local radio that he had "no reason to go to parliament... There is no sense in the president going to debate these issues, because that is what the deputies are for."
